blocks.text: Separating one or two components from a simple mixture needs simple techniques such as filtration, distillation and solvent extraction, but complex mixtures need more powerful ones. Chromatography is a versatile and important analytical technique that separates the individual components of a complex mixture according to their different affinities for two phases. Complex mixtures, such as the dyes in flowers, pollutants in a water body or medicinal extracts from leaves, can be separated this way. Chromatography is used to identify, purify and measure substances with high precision, which makes it an efficient modern analytical tool in medicine, forensic science and environmental science.

blocks.alt: A green leaf extract, and next to it a strip in a tube with coloured bands labelled, from top to bottom, carotene, xanthophyll, chlorophyll a, chlorophyll b and pheophytin.
blocks.caption: Separating the pigments of a leaf (original sketch after Figure 28.1).
blocks.long_description: A single green extract contains several pigments. Because each pigment is held back by the two phases to a different extent, they travel different distances and form separate coloured bands.

blocks.title: Stationary and mobile phases
blocks.text: In chromatography the mixture is shared between a stationary phase, which stays in place (a solid or a liquid held on a solid), and a mobile phase, which moves past it (a liquid solvent or a gas). Components that prefer the mobile phase travel further or faster.

Adsorption is a surface effect in which particles collect only on the outer surface of a solid; activated charcoal, for example, adsorbs gases and impurities on its surface, which is why it is used in filters. Of the many types of chromatography, three important ones are paper chromatography (PC), thin-layer chromatography (TLC) and gas chromatography (GC).

blocks.prompt: What decides how far each component of a mixture travels in chromatography?
blocks.explanation: Its relative affinity for the stationary and mobile phases: the more it prefers the mobile phase, the further (or faster) it moves.

items: Chromatography separates mixtures by different affinities for a stationary and a mobile phase.
